paragraphs: But in the drawing-room the talk was already over. Katerina Ivanovna was very worked up, though she looked determined. Just as Alyosha and Madame Hohlakov walked in, Ivan Fyodorovitch got up to say goodbye. His face was a little pale, and Alyosha watched him anxiously. This moment would settle a doubt that had been nagging at him, a riddle that had haunted him for some time. Over the past month, people had hinted to him more than once that his brother Ivan was in love with Katerina Ivanovna. Worse, they said he meant “to carry her off” from Dmitri. Until very recently the idea had struck Alyosha as monstrous, though it troubled him badly. He loved both his brothers, and he dreaded a rivalry between them. And only the day before, Dmitri had said straight out that he was glad Ivan was his rival, and that it was a great help to him, Dmitri. How was it a help? Toward marrying Grushenka? But Alyosha thought that the worst thing that could happen. There was more. Until the evening before, Alyosha had taken it for granted that Katerina Ivanovna loved Dmitri with a steady, passionate love. But he had believed it only until the evening before. He had also supposed that she could never love a man like Ivan, that she loved Dmitri, and loved him exactly as he was, however strange such a passion might be.

But during yesterday’s scene with Grushenka another thought had struck him. The word “lacerating,” which Madame Hohlakov had just used, nearly made him start. Half awake toward dawn that night, he had cried out “Laceration, laceration,” most likely about his dream. He had dreamed all night about the previous day’s scene at Katerina Ivanovna’s. Now Madame Hohlakov’s blunt, insistent claim impressed him: Katerina Ivanovna was in love with Ivan, and was only fooling herself with a pose, out of “self-laceration.” She tormented herself with a pretended love for Dmitri, out of some imagined duty of gratitude. “Yes,” he thought, “perhaps the whole truth is in those words.” But if so, where did that leave Ivan? Alyosha sensed that a character like Katerina Ivanovna’s had to rule, and that she could rule only a man like Dmitri, never a man like Ivan. Dmitri might in the end give in to her rule “to his own happiness” (which was just what Alyosha wished for). But Ivan—no, Ivan could not give in to her, and giving in would not make him happy. Alyosha could not help believing that about Ivan. All these doubts and reflections flitted through his mind as he came into the drawing-room. And another thought pressed itself on him: “What if she loved neither of them—neither Ivan nor Dmitri?”

It should be said that Alyosha felt almost ashamed of these thoughts, and blamed himself whenever they kept coming back during the past month. “What do I know about love and women, and how can I settle such questions?” he would think reproachfully, after such doubts and guesses. And yet he could not help thinking about it. He sensed that this rivalry mattered enormously in his brothers’ lives and that a great deal hung on it.

“One reptile will devour the other,” Ivan had said the day before, speaking angrily of their father and Dmitri. So Ivan saw Dmitri as a reptile, and perhaps had for a long time. Perhaps ever since he had known Katerina Ivanovna? Of course, the phrase had slipped out of Ivan yesterday without his meaning it, but that only made it more important. If he felt that way, what hope was there of peace? Were there not, rather, fresh grounds for hatred and hostility in their family? And whose side was Alyosha to take? And what was he to wish for each of them? He loved them both. But what could he wish for either one, with their interests clashing like this? He could lose his way completely in this maze, and Alyosha’s heart could not stand uncertainty, because his love was always active. He could not love passively. When he loved someone, he set to work at once to help him. To do that, he had to know what he was aiming at. He had to know for certain what was best for each of them, and once he knew, it came naturally to him to help them both. But instead of a clear aim, he found only uncertainty and confusion on every side. “It was lacerating,” as had just been said. But what could he make of even this “laceration”? He could not understand the first word of this baffling maze.

When she saw Alyosha, Katerina Ivanovna said quickly and happily to Ivan, who was already on his feet to leave, “One minute! Stay just one more minute! I want to hear what this person here thinks. I trust him completely. Don’t go,” she added, to Madame Hohlakov. She made Alyosha sit down beside her, while Madame Hohlakov sat across from them, next to Ivan.

“You are all my friends here, all I have in the world, my dear friends,” she began warmly, her voice trembling with real tears of suffering. Alyosha’s heart went out to her at once. “Alexey Fyodorovitch, you saw that abominable scene yesterday, and you saw what I did. You didn’t see it, Ivan Fyodorovitch, but he did. What he thought of me yesterday, I don’t know. I know only this: if it happened again today, this very minute, I would show the same feelings as yesterday—the same feelings, the same words, the same actions. You remember what I did, Alexey Fyodorovitch. You held me back from one thing” ... (as she said that, she flushed and her eyes shone). “I have to tell you, I can’t get over it. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I don’t even know whether I still love _him_. I feel _pity_ for him, and that is a poor sign of love. If I loved him, if I still loved him, maybe I wouldn’t pity him now. I would hate him.”
Her voice trembled, and tears glittered on her lashes. Alyosha shuddered inside. “This girl is honest and sincere,” he thought, “and she doesn’t love Dmitri any more.”
“That’s true, that’s true,” cried Madame Hohlakov.

“Wait, dear. I haven’t yet told you the main thing, the final decision I reached during the night. I feel that my decision may be a terrible one—for me. But I can see that nothing will make me change it—nothing. It will be so all my life. My dear, kind, ever-faithful, generous adviser, the one friend I have in the world, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who sees so deep into the heart, approves my decision and praises it. He knows what it is.”
“Yes, I approve of it,” Ivan agreed, in a quiet but firm voice.

“But I would like Alyosha, too, to tell me (Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, forgive me for calling you just Alyosha), I would like Alexey Fyodorovitch, too, to tell me in front of my two friends whether I am right. I feel instinctively that you, Alyosha, my dear brother (for you are a dear brother to me),” she said again, in a rapture, taking his cold hand in her hot one, “I can see that your verdict, your approval, will give me peace in spite of all my suffering. After your words, I will be calm and I will submit—I feel it.”

“I don’t know what you’re asking of me,” said Alyosha, blushing. “All I know is that I love you, and right now I want your happiness more than my own!... But I know nothing about such things,” something made him add in a rush.

“In such things, Alexey Fyodorovitch, in such things, what counts most is honor and duty and something higher—I don’t know what—maybe even higher than duty. I feel this irresistible feeling in my heart, and it drives me on irresistibly. But it can all be said in two words. I have already decided. Even if he marries that—creature,” she began solemnly, “whom I never, never can forgive, _even then I will not abandon him_. From now on I will never, never abandon him!” she cried, breaking into a kind of pale, hysterical ecstasy. “Not that I would chase after him all the time, or get in his way and plague him. Oh, no! I will go away to another town—wherever you like—but I will watch over him all my life—I will watch over him all my life, without ever stopping. When he becomes unhappy with that woman, and that is bound to happen very soon, let him come to me. He will find a friend, a sister.... Only a sister, of course, and so for ever. But at least he will learn that this sister really is his sister, who loves him and has given up her whole life for him. I will get my way. I will make him know me and trust me completely, holding nothing back,” she cried, in a kind of frenzy. “I will be a god for him to pray to—and that, at least, he owes me, for his treachery and for what I suffered yesterday because of him. And let him see that all my life I will be true to him and to the promise I made him, even though he was untrue and betrayed me. I will—I will turn myself into nothing but a means to his happiness, or—how can I put it?—an instrument, a machine for his happiness, and that for my whole life, my whole life, and let him see that all his life! That is my decision. Ivan Fyodorovitch fully approves.”

She was out of breath. Perhaps she had meant to put her idea with more dignity, more art and more naturalness, but her speech came out too hurried and crude. It was full of youthful impulse. It showed that she was still smarting from yesterday’s insult, and that her pride wanted satisfaction. She felt this herself. Her face suddenly darkened, and an ugly look came into her eyes. Alyosha saw it at once and felt a pang of sympathy. His brother Ivan made things worse by adding:

“I have only given my own view,” he said. “From anyone else this would seem put on and overwrought. From you it does not. Any other woman would be wrong, but you are right. I can’t explain it, but I see that you are completely genuine, and therefore you are right.”
“But that’s only for the moment. And what is this moment worth? Nothing but yesterday’s insult.” Madame Hohlakov plainly had not meant to meddle, but she could not hold back this very fair remark.

“Quite so, quite so,” cried Ivan, with odd eagerness, clearly annoyed at the interruption. “In anyone else this moment would come only from yesterday’s impression and would be only a moment. But with Katerina Ivanovna’s character, that moment will last her whole life. What would be a mere promise for anyone else is for her a lifelong duty. It is heavy, perhaps grim, but it will never let up. And she will be held up by the feeling that she is fulfilling it. Katerina Ivanovna, from now on your life will be spent in painful brooding over your own feelings, your own heroism, your own suffering. But in the end that suffering will soften, and turn into a sweet contemplation of a bold and proud design carried out. Yes, proud it certainly is, and desperate in any case, but a triumph for you. And knowing that will at last be a source of complete satisfaction, and will make you resigned to everything else.”
This was said unmistakably with some malice, and clearly on purpose. Perhaps he did not even want to hide that he was being ironical and meant it so.
“Oh dear, it’s all so mistaken!” Madame Hohlakov cried again.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, you speak. I am dying to know what you will say!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, and burst into tears. Alyosha got up from the sofa.

“It’s nothing, nothing!” she went on through her tears. “I’m upset, I didn’t sleep last night. But with two such friends beside me as you and your brother, I still feel strong—for I know—you two will never desert me.”
“Unfortunately I have to go back to Moscow—maybe tomorrow—and leave you for a long time—And unfortunately, there is no avoiding it,” Ivan said suddenly.

“Tomorrow—to Moscow!” Her face twisted suddenly. “But—but, good heavens, how lucky!” she cried, in a voice that had suddenly changed. In an instant there was no trace of her tears. She was transformed in a moment, and it astonished Alyosha. Instead of a poor, insulted girl, weeping in a kind of “laceration,” he saw a woman fully in command of herself, and even extremely pleased, as if something delightful had just happened.

“Oh, not lucky that I’m losing you, of course not,” she corrected herself suddenly, with a charming society smile. “A friend like you could never think that. I am only too unhappy to lose you.” She rushed impulsively up to Ivan, seized both his hands and pressed them warmly. “What is lucky is that in Moscow you will be able to see auntie and Agafya and tell them all the horror of my situation now. You can speak with complete openness to Agafya, but go easy on dear auntie. You will know how. You can’t think how miserable I was yesterday and this morning, wondering how I could write them that dreadful letter—for one can never tell such things in a letter.... Now it will be easy for me to write, because you will see them and explain everything. Oh, how glad I am! But I am glad only of that, believe me. Of course, no one can take your place.... I will run and write the letter right now,” she finished suddenly, and took a step as though to leave the room.
